paragraphs.text: The word of God is a fountain of light. Full of light and shining out light, it illuminates the minds of the faithful and flashes all around them. It shines from itself and in itself, and floods with radiance those who enjoy it. It does not only illuminate the mind of the faithful; it also bestows on them the name of light. For divine Scripture rightly calls "darkness" those who are raised on ignorance and live with unbelief, who do not receive the torch of truth so as to become sons of light. That is why the divine apostle Paul says: "We are not sons of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day." And we truly are sons of light, we who belong to the gospel word spoken by the mouth of God. "For I am," says Christ, "the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." That is a word of light, and if we believe it, it makes us ready to become sons of light. Hence the Savior also says: "While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become sons of light." As this visible light is to bodies, so the spiritual word of God is to souls; and what darkness is in the night, ignorance is in souls that have gone astray. For this reason blessed David writes about such people: "They have not known, nor understood; they walk about in darkness." In the same way God calls the synagogue "night": it is steeped in ignorance and unwilling to lift its head toward the knowledge of spiritual teaching, and ignorance lives with it. When God said to the Jews through the prophet, "I have likened your mother to night," he explained what kind of night he meant, a night like darkness, and added: "My people has become like a people that has no knowledge." Therefore: "They have not known, nor understood; they walk about in night." So it is with them. But those who have received the light of Christ's teaching are themselves made light. For our God is light. His Word, begotten from him impassibly before the ages, is called light. And the holy, consubstantial and life-originating Spirit is light. Light, and light, and light, yet one light. And the soul that has received the Word is called light. But God is light by nature, in three hypostases, while we are light by sharing in him. Again, our Lord Jesus Christ himself is light, of whom the evangelist John says: "He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world." Being light from ineffable light, he also sends forth the law full of light, as the prophet says: "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." So the soul that has received the luminous word of truth itself becomes light, and hears from Paul: "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." When the mind receives the light of the gospel, it is called light by virtue of its faith, and likewise by virtue of its works. "Let your light shine before people," he says, "so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." Whoever has received the light of faith must go on to works of light. The believer's soul must not only be light; it must also shine before people by its works. That is why the Savior says: "Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." And see the wonder of it. The light that comes from God is simple, yet it has various rays, different not by nature but in their workings. The shining teaching of God is sent upon every faithful soul, as it is said: "And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us," so that our works may be directed by him. The brightness is one, but when it comes to us it produces many brightnesses: the brightness of almsgiving, the brightness of chastity, the brightness of hospitality, the brightness of tender affection. With God there is one brightness; but sent to us, it produces in its workings a variety of gleams. To one it grants the brightness of prophecy, to another the brightness of apostleship, to another the brightness of martyrdom. There it is one brightness; with us it is many, as it is said: "With you is sovereignty in the day of your power, in the brightnesses of your saints." Why then does Paul make a list and say: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?" Paul does not divide them arbitrarily. As God finds souls suited, he distributes his gifts, not by bare authority but according to the confession of faith. It is not that he gives against his own wish or will, but that his will is not indiscriminate; it follows the graces of the gifts. Think of the bright, richly dyed fabrics of a royal robe. They receive a single ray of sunlight, yet send out a variety of gleams, and whatever the beauty of the dye, such is the brilliant color it produces. The beauty of the very air is, as it were, dyed anew by the dye before it, into gold or purple or green or some other color. The ray is not divided; rather, the robe shapes in the light how the ray is disposed. With flowers like these the beauty of the church always shines. She wears a royal robe and is arrayed in a heavenly, many-colored garment, as the psalmist says: "Daughters of kings are among your honored ones; the queen stands at your right hand, clothed in a robe of gold, arrayed in many colors." How is she arrayed in many colors? With the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in Paul's words: "God working with signs and wonders and various powers, and with distributions of the Holy Spirit." But what shall I call the church of Christ? An adorned bride, a beautified queen, a luxuriant paradise, a meadow teeming with fruit? Whatever else I might say would fall short of her worth. That is why the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of the church and taking up her voice, said: "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation." And since he was speaking in a figure and could not express the church's whole beauty, he added variety to the image, saying: "He has adorned me with ornaments like a bride, and put a headdress on me like a bridegroom, and like the earth making its produce grow, and like a garden its seeds of herbs." For the church of the living God truly is a garden enclosed and a paradise. When I say paradise, I do not mean one like that ancient paradise, but one far higher. For there the serpent reigned, but here Christ reigns.

Do not look to the prestige of the name, but to the power of the reality. A paradise is not wonderful unless God's commandment is kept in it, and humble places are not dishonored if God's law reigns in them. Which is better, which is superior: paradise or a dunghill? Yet paradise was no help to Adam, because of his transgression, and the dunghill did Job no harm, because of his endurance. Adam is put to shame in paradise for his disobedience; Job is crowned on the dunghill for his endurance. The prestige of a place never counts for anything unless a good will goes with it. Heaven is higher than paradise, yet the devil falls from there. The earth lies low and heaven is raised on high, yet the devil falls from heaven for his transgression, as it says, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven," while the poor are lifted up from the earth, as it says, "He raises the poor from the earth, and lifts the needy from the dunghill." Do you see that it is not the difference of places that wins us advantages, but everywhere it is faith and endurance and hope that weave crowns for the worthy? Nothing is more respectable than a bedchamber, nothing more exposed than a theater. What good did adultery in the bedchamber do the licentious Egyptian woman? What harm did it do Thecla, the first woman martyr, to wrestle naked in the theater? She did not sin by being stripped; the saint is not dishonored but crowned. The one is crowned in the theater; the other is pilloried in the bridal chamber. What good did the idols do, or the worship of things that do not exist? I mean the grandeur of the temples. And what harm did the humbleness of their tombs do the martyrs? Was not error put to shame in its grandeur, and was not the martyrs' cause exalted in humility? So the church of the living God is a paradise of delight. In that paradise the serpent danced and deceived. In this paradise the Savior says: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you." In that paradise the way of life was shut to Adam because of his transgression. And to show that the virtuous soul is not hindered, God lets it receive outside paradise greater things than those in paradise. Paradise is closed to Adam, and Peter is entrusted with the keys of heaven. Adam is cast out of paradise, and Paul is caught up to the third heaven. The tree of life is walled off from Adam, for, it says, God said: "Lest Adam touch the tree of life." There life was barred, and the tree of life was barred to the transgressor. Here the tree of the cross has been planted, and all who wish may harvest eternal life. In paradise after the transgression Adam hides from God, struck by his conscience. He who searches out all things calls to him and says: "Adam, where are you?" Did he not know where he was? "Adam, where are you?" He says "Where are you?" to convict him of his lawlessness, meaning "What state are you in? Did the serpent's deceit bring you equality with God? Do you see how you have been stripped naked? Where are you?" "I heard your voice, and I hid." Adam hides in paradise, while the apostles say: "We all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, from glory to glory." Do you see boldness outside paradise? Do you see shame inside paradise? In paradise after the transgression God clothed Adam in garments of skin. Let us see what we have been clothed in. There he put on a tunic; here, as many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There, when paradise was shut, the cherubim and the turning sword barred the way into paradise. It was like a wall and a barrier to Adam, not allowing him to enter because of the disobedience he had committed in paradise. I do not say this to accuse paradise, but because that place, worthy of God, was of no help to one who chose not to live with a good will. A wall of fire encircled paradise and would not let the transgressor enter. In this way God showed that it was not the fire that was hostile to Adam; his transgression kept him from passing through the wall of fire. Indeed, a chariot of fire caught Elijah up into heaven. The church of God does not lie when she says: "God has clothed me with the garment of salvation, and adorned me with ornaments like a bride, like the earth making its produce grow." This great paradise, the universal church, is a great garden of truth. Christ reigns in it and is trusted as its lawgiver, unless perhaps someone in the church is found sick with heretical error from the teaching of serpents (I mean the error of heresy); such a person is cast out of here, as Adam was out of paradise. There the man who was persuaded by the serpent's teaching was banished from paradise. So too in the church, those who do not obey Paul and are not taught by Peter, but are persuaded by the teachings of serpents, are cast out of this paradise. How is this clear? Paul says: "I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted." But the serpent's teaching has no place here, since the great shepherd crushes the serpents' heads with the staff of faith. As a shepherd, our admirable father crushes the heads of the dragons with the faith of the gospel and with hope in Christ. As an excellent planter and gardener, he nourishes the plants of the church and roots out any bastard seed or shoot. The disease of impiety, the error of paganism, he hands over to the fire like thorns. Heretical error he plucks out like couch grass and throws away, for he is clothed with a zeal for God that most people do not understand. For some people make a habit of using clever arguments against the church and the holy shepherds, as they do against this admirable father. Many bring in idleness under the guise of moderation, insult zeal, and try to blunt the vigorous word of God. You can find someone saying, under the guise of moderation: "What do we have to do with the pagans? Does he want to be saved? Let him be saved." Whoever says this has never yet been wounded by zeal for godliness. Whoever sees someone perishing and does not mourn his destruction, does not count it as his own loss, does not know the zeal of godliness and has not been wounded by the arrows of truth.

So whoever sees someone perishing and is not moved with zeal is no disciple of Paul. Paul says somewhere: "Who is weak, and I am not weak?" Let such a person compare the achievements of our father, and he will find him in harmony with the apostle's words: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" Those who think this way are brothers of the apostles. For the righteous man is downcast not only over his own sins but also when he sees others sinning, as David says: "Despondency seized me because of sinners who forsake your law." Whoever is downcast over other people's sins has zeal for godliness. While the righteous man is setting his own life right, he weeps and mourns in order to wipe out his own sin. Then, once he has ceased from his own sin, he goes on to mourn the sins of others, as Paul does: "I fear that when I come I may have to mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." Paul mourns those who sinned and did not repent. Samuel mourns Saul, so that God says: "How long will you mourn over Saul?" You see a soul perishing and you do not mourn? If someone sees a dead man being carried out and does not weep, he is shown to be harsh, hard and brutish. If you see a soul drowning in impiety, condemned to eternal death and persisting in unbelief, tell me, do you not weep and mourn? Is that the mark of a devout soul? The right-minded person must mourn all other sins, but above all when he sees a soul steeped in the impiety of paganism. Over such a soul one must not only mourn but burn and be set on fire with zeal, so as to become a disciple of Paul. For, it says, "while Paul was staying in Athens, his spirit was set on fire within him as he saw that the city was full of idols." Why do the saints think this way, just as this admirable father was a defender of godliness? A king on earth holds the world that is under him, and has advocates in every court of his palace; in the same way God has faithful shepherds as defenders of godliness. Pagans often scoff when they hear Christians saying to them, "Why do you blaspheme? Why are you impious?" At once they jeer: "Look, God's avengers! Can't God avenge himself?" He does not avenge himself, for the Godhead is not harmed by insult. Instead he scourges ungrateful slaves through faithful household servants. Does God need avengers? Yes: not because he is weak, but to open a door of zeal for you. If he did everything by himself, the way of life would be shut to the zealous. Did not Pharaoh once fight against God, sunk deep in impiety, and no scourge was brought on him until faithful Moses came forward? Did not polytheistic error flourish with its false priests and false prophets, and no blow came from God until Elijah the zealot came forward? The saints are, beyond dispute, God's avengers. That is why Paul says: "We are ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete." There is also Deborah, admirable among women. She had a woman's weakness, yet prophesied with manly virtue, and of her Scripture says: "Deborah arose, a mother in Israel." She became a mother of the people through godliness, and was so strong that when war came the generals with Barak said to her: "If you do not come to war with us, we will not go." They were not relying on the woman's courage but on the power of prophecy. Many went out as co-workers of God's counsel and cut down the foreigners. Then blessed Deborah, bearing the truth, says: "Lord, those who love you are like the rising of the sun, but your enemies are like the snuff of a lamp." "Lord, those who love you are like the rising of the sun," because the sun is never put out. "But your enemies are like the snuff of a lamp," because a lamp's light lasts only for a time and then goes out. Then she praises the general who served God's counsel, and after that she orders a curse on the inhabitants of Meroz, because they did not come out to the help of the Lord. Did God need help, then? Yes. Those who help godliness must be brought to light. In the same way this admirable father does not help God as though God were feeble. He has been appointed to this task, and he defends godliness, showing himself in body [exposed?] to destruction, but laying hold of souls for [God's?] dominion [?]. For "the arrows of the mighty are sharpened." And do not be surprised that the shepherds of Christ and teachers of godliness defend the truth. Even someone who is not a teacher and has not been entrusted with a teacher's throne, but has simply received Christ's word and stands in the rank of a disciple, ought to have zeal for God. He should repay his benefactor by speaking freely, speaking out for the truth and contending against impiety, so that he may hear from holy Scripture: "Child, contend for the truth, and the Lord God will fight for you." It is no surprise that saints defend godliness. Often God, being good, uses gentle language out of forbearance, and the prophets do not let godliness be wounded by God's forbearance. God says through Moses: "Say to Pharaoh: Let my people go. But if you will not, behold, I will send the signs and strike you." Moses was struck by the word, and a thought was given to the godly man, as if to say: "Do not suppose that Pharaoh has a people on an equal footing with God's people." He was anxious that God's great goodness and forbearance might do Pharaoh harm, and that on hearing "your people" and "my people" he might think himself God's rival. So Moses modifies the proclamation: "Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: Let my people go. But if you will not, behold, I will send the signs and strike you and your servants, so that you may know that the earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it." [?] heard "people" and "people", but did not follow the wording; instead he says: "The whole earth is the Lord's." Even if God used forbearance, Moses does not betray the Master's authority. Indeed, God spoke this way so that the godly man's zeal might be laid bare. The faithful always love to go beyond God's words. The Savior says to the disciples: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" One of his disciples says: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Let the zeal of the Holy Spirit teach you too to be zealous, to suffer for godliness, and to fight the good fight for righteousness.

For it is fitting that good disciples should imitate their teacher, as Paul also says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." Do you want to learn that even someone who is simply a disciple, who holds only a disciple's rank, ought to have zeal for godliness? Hear how Christ healed the man blind from birth. Or rather, let us hear the story itself from the beginning. After the evangelist had said a great deal, he began to speak like this: "As Jesus passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, saying," and so on. "And he spat, made clay, anointed his eyes, and said to him: Go, wash in the pool of Siloam. And when he had washed, he received his sight." The Jews recognized him and said: "Is this not the man who used to sit begging for alms, because he was blind?" Some said, "Yes"; others, "No, but he is like him." He himself said, "I am the man." But the Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews saw that the miracle had drawn many to Christ. Stung by the zeal of their ungodliness and pricked by the goad of truth, they called in the man who had once been blind. And there was a wicked spectacle to be seen: godliness being championed, wicked judges sitting in judgment, a great advocate joining in the contest, and God presiding as umpire and looking on. The children of the Jews called in the man who had once been blind and now saw, stood him in the middle of the council, and said to him: "Tell us how you received your sight, who opened your eyes, and what he did to you." They said this not to learn anything, but to frighten him by the way they put the question. For the way a question is put often teaches the person questioned whether to answer or keep silent. Suppose someone says to a man about to testify about some matter: "Do you know the case? Were you there? How do you know about it?" The very form of the question teaches him to deny everything. So it was with them: "How did you receive your sight? Who opened your eyes?" But he cared less about the threat and held all the more firmly to the truth, and said: "A man called Jesus made clay, anointed my eyes, and said to me, 'Go, wash in Siloam.' So I went and washed, and I received my sight." He did not know the truth, but he acknowledged the benefit he had received; he did not yet know the dignity of his benefactor. "A man made clay and anointed my eyes, and I see." The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight until they called the parents of the man who had received it. Malice raised its objection and brought the truth into doubt. They called the blind man's parents. Malice gathers witnesses against itself. The parents of the blind man were called. Again the question was put in the same way: "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?" The parents understood the manner of their malice, that they were making threats, and said: "We know that this is our son, and we know that he was born blind; but how he now sees, or who opened his eyes, we do not know. He is of age; ask him. He will speak for himself." And see the wisdom of God. In the ordinary law courts the testimony of the man who had received his sight could have been set aside, either because he was young or because he did not know how to speak. So that they could not do this, God arranged that he should first be shown to be of legal age. "He is of age," they say; "ask him." For minors need advocates, but those of full age become their own advocates. His parents answered and said: "This is our son, and we know that he was born blind." The parents confessed this so that there would be no room to doubt that he had been blind. "He is of age; ask him. He will speak for himself." "So they called him," it says, "a second time, and said to him: What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" Now, clothed in zeal for God, he spurned the question. Judging them unworthy of an answer, he did not deign to reply. Instead, what did he say to them? "I have told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear me again? Do you too want to become his disciples?" So he imitated the teaching of Christ, though he had not yet heard the teaching of Christ. For at the Feast of Dedication the Jews surrounded the Savior in Solomon's portico and said to him: "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." He said to them: "I told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear again?" And see the godliness of the advocate. He noticed the malice of the Jews: they were doing everything they could, and putting on a show of brandishing threats and fear at him, to keep him from confessing Jesus as his teacher. So he said to them: "I have told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear again? Do you too want to become his disciples?" By saying "Do you too?" he showed that his own discipleship was openly admitted. Let every Christian who has come out of paganism keep these words ready. When a pagan who clings to the ancient habit of error meets you and says, "You have become a Christian," say to him: "Yes. Do you want to become one too?" Such, then, was the aim of the man who had received his sight in both soul and body. "I have told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear me again? Do you too want to become his disciples?" In other words: "You are so far from changing my mind that I expect you to change instead and confess that he is the Christ." Then what did the Jews say to him? "They reviled him and said: You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from." Consider how many spoke against him, and the strength of the one man who stood up to them. Once again the advocate of the truth did not keep silent. He stood firm, and this is what makes it marvelous, saying: "You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing." He stood there contending, with God as overseer and umpire: many fierce opponents against one strong man, a cloud of unbelief against a single drop of faith. "Never since the world began," he says, "has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing." He means: "Since you pride yourselves on the teaching of Moses..." For the moment he does not mention Moses, so as not to provoke them. But he says: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind." That is: what other prophet ever opened them? Yet they could not see Christ's superiority, or that there was no comparison. The more firmly he held to the truth, the more they persisted in their shamelessness. Since they could not deny the miracle, they now tried hard to cover it up, and said: "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." The glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, and that glory is undivided. He contends, fighting the good fight against the Jews. They say to him: "Give glory to God." To which God? The God of our law? And is it right for one to confer the benefit and another to be glorified? "Give glory to God." One is my benefactor, and am I to give the glory to another? They admitted that Jesus made clay and anointed his eyes. The one who opened them is acknowledged, and shall I ascribe the glory to someone else? And why should I give glory to God? Because this work is God's. So you admit, against your will, that Christ is God. "Give glory to God." For if the work is God's, the glory is owed to him as well; the one who did the work is himself God. "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." The man who had once been blind answered them: "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see."

Since he had spoken so boldly up to this point, they ordered him to be thrown out. "And they threw him out," says the evangelist. "Blessed is the one who is cut off from the assembly of evildoers." And see what happens. He had fought the good fight. He had pleaded for the glory of God and confessed the Savior gloriously and with great boldness, and the arena was filled with his bouts. Then the wrestler was thrown out without receiving the crown, and outside the umpire comes to meet him. "For Jesus heard," it says, "that they had thrown him out, and when he found him he said to him..." What a word, "when he found him"! The one whom error loses, truth finds. Why did he come to meet him? The Savior saw a soul full of gratitude. He saw a soul that did not yet realize it was speaking on God's behalf, but thought it was speaking for some faithful prophet. For when he was asked about Christ, what did he say about him? That he is a prophet. So the Savior said to himself: "If he contends like this while he thinks I am a prophet and takes me for a man, what will he not do when he learns the glory of the Godhead?" He took Christ for a man and called him a prophet, yet he offered such a defense of the truth and took up so great a contest. He had not yet been instructed in the faith, but was enlightened only by the benefit he had received. Consider him: if he did not depart from the truth while thinking he was pleading for a man, what will happen when he learns to say, in the words of the Gospel, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"? That is why the Savior then guided him on to knowledge, accepting his contest and putting the seal on his faith. The Savior comes to meet him, for the man did not recognize his features. When Jesus sent him to the pool of Siloam to wash, he sent a blind man. When the man came back seeing, he did not see the Savior, who was mingled with the crowd. Instead, before he could see the Master, he was immediately called into the contest and fought it. Before he washed, the Master had made clay and anointed his eyes, to fill up what was lacking. So when they threw him out, Christ found him and said to him: "Do you believe in the Son of God?" That is: you must not believe as though you were contending for a prophet, but for the Son of God. The man did not recognize the face, but he recognized the voice. "Do you believe," he says, "in the Son of God?" He recognized the voice and cried out with great joy: "And who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" [?] As if to say: "Why do you ask me, faithful one, 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' I know that your word is true; and if you tell me who he is, I will not hesitate to believe you." "And who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" And the one who foreknows all things replied: "You have seen him, and he is the one speaking with you." The one who had pleaded the case inside now converses outside. "Do you believe in the Son of God?" And the man, enlightened in both body and mind, said: "And who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" He answered him: "You have seen him, and he is the one speaking with you." And he said: "Lord, I believe"; and he worshiped him. I have said these things so that all of you may learn to follow a good teacher, to imitate a good shepherd, and to contend for the truth. For your contest is carried on with the help of the great Shepherd. You were amazed that a blind man became an advocate of the truth after he had received a benefit. Be amazed, then, at the thief who pleaded for Christ before he received any benefit. For a godly soul that is zealous for the truth always, by its own trustworthiness, opens many mouths to plead for the truth. Christ was hanging on the cross with two thieves, one on his right and one on his left. The Jews were babbling and the high priests blaspheming: "Look, the King of the Jews!" And again: "If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him." And again: "He saved others; he cannot save himself." In the same way the thief crucified with him also babbled: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us." But the other thief said nothing, and his silence rebuked the condemned. The high priests and the scribes knew the law, or rather were ignorant of it. They ought to have confessed Christ from the readings of the prophets, and they did not. So God opened an unexpected mouth on the cross to plead for the truth. And see what he does. He has not even heard a word from Christ first, yet he pleads for him, and then he is crowned. "For two thieves," it says, "were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left." The Savior was in the middle like the beam of a scale of truth, lifting up the one who confesses and condemning the one who blasphemes. And see the wonder. The scribes and high priests were blaspheming Christ, saying: "If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him." The other thief was saying: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us." Yet the grateful thief said nothing. For the two thieves were images of the Jewish people and of our own. The one blasphemes and is condemned; the other believes, repents, and is saved. So the brother of the ungrateful, the one who shared in the brigandage of the Jews, speaks. For the ungrateful Jews were a people of robbers, as the Savior testifies when he says: "My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers." The disposition of the first thief was Jewish. That of the second was Christian: it set out from evil, but seized salvation by repentance. So the ungrateful thief, with his Jewish disposition, said: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us" by coming down from the cross. But the other proved grateful. In the courtroom he had been the accused; on the cross he became the judge, and a teacher of the fear of God as well. For the thief's first words to his fellow thief are: "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence? And we indeed are suffering justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong." What are you saying? You who stole out there, do you pass sentence here? You who murdered out there, do you teach the fear of God here? "Do you not even fear God?" Learn about the cross of Christ, so that this voice may become your teacher of godliness. For see the wonder: the thief says to his fellow thief, "Do you not even fear God?" He proclaims as God the one who was crucified with them of his own will and was patiently suffering for humanity. And if you want to know that he is speaking of the Savior himself when he says, "Do you not even fear God?", learn it from what follows: "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence? And we indeed are suffering justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong." I say these things so that you may learn to labor for godliness, to show your zeal both at home and in the marketplace, and to contend for Christ. Then you too will receive the crown of righteousness from him, like this grateful thief. For listen to what he says to his blaspheming fellow thief: "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence? And we indeed are suffering justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong." And he said to Jesus: "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom." Do you see true advocacy? Do you see how he confessed Christ himself as true God? "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom." He confesses his own crimes and pleads for the Master. Thief, you were tortured so severely before the governor to make you confess the robberies, murders, and thefts you had committed, and still you did not confess. Yet here, without torture, you say: "We are receiving what our deeds deserve"? Before the governor you hardly confessed even under countless tortures. Here, with no one forcing you, do you confess so readily? "Yes," he says, "for there death follows confession, but here repentance and life follow confession. We are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong." "If we suffer justly," he says, "this man suffers unjustly. We murdered the living; he raised the dead. We plundered what belonged to others; he has given his own wealth to the world." The thief fights with his fellow thief and says: "Until now, until this moment on the cross, we came together and traveled together. But now, from the cross, my road parts from yours. If you want to travel with me to life, come. If not, go your own way. Before, when I traveled with you, I was on the first road with you. But now the cross has split this second road in two." Through repentance the road of the thieves divides. And the psalm, the end of the psalm, was then being fulfilled: "The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish." So when the thief had pleaded for the truth, he turned to the King of glory and said: "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom."

So let the Arians be ashamed, and let them hear what the thief says: "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom." The thief sees him crucified and confesses him as Lord; the heretic confesses that he shares the Father's throne and yet blasphemes him as a creature. "Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom." I would like to say something to the thief: "Why should Christ remember you? What worthy thing have you done? That you murdered? That you robbed? Yet you say, 'Remember me when you come into your kingdom.'" But let no one think that Christ saved the thief by grace alone; no, it was owed to him as a debt. "What debt?" someone says. "That he acted justly? That he gave alms? That he shared out his goods, fasted, kept vigils? Did he do something no one else did? Or was it that he believed in God? The prophets too believed in God, and the patriarchs believed, the psalmists believed, the apostles, the preachers, the martyrs." Yes, but all of them saw God in glory, while this man saw him in disgrace. Picture ten thousand servants serving a master while the master is prospering and honored, and one slave who does not leave his own master in a time of trial, affliction and flight, while those ten thousand slaves desert their master in the time of trial and flight and slip away. Can those slaves who served the master in his prosperity and deserted him in the time of trial be equal to the one who followed his master in his misfortune? Not at all. Peter believed, but he believed after seeing him raise the dead and beholding his glory. Paul believed, but after seeing light from heaven, light that blinded his bodily eyes and enlightened the eyes of his soul. Abraham believed, but after seeing a divine vision. Isaiah believed, but after seeing him seated on a lofty throne with the cherubim around him. All of them saw him, but in glory; this man saw him in disgrace. That is why he cried out, "Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom." You ought to tell me, from your own case [?]: why do you say this? "Because I am a sinner and a murderer, a thief up to this very hour. My crimes are many, I confess it. But I have a faith hidden in my mind that no one knows except the Master alone, who suffers with me. Outwardly the Master bears the visible signs of his passion; but I," he says, "paid no attention to the visible disgrace. I glorify the hidden kingdom." So you too should say: "Lord, do not look at my visible wrongdoings but at my hidden faith, and remember me when you come into your kingdom." Christ, who had said nothing at all to anyone but had kept silent, answering neither Pilate nor any other ungrateful soul among the Jews, answers now; and since it would have been very harsh and out of place to stay silent, he answers at last and says to the thief, "Truly, truly, I tell you: today you will be with me in paradise." O the grace of the benefactor! "Since you asked for a slow grace, saying, 'Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom,' you asked for a slow one, but I give a swift grace: today you will be with me in paradise." Do you see God's salvation? Do you see the Master's kindness? Do you see the great judge of truth? "Today you will be with me in paradise." Before this, no one among the Jews or the patriarchs had heard a promise of paradise, from the time Adam transgressed and went out of it. God made countless promises to faithful people, yet he promised paradise to no one but the thief. Nowhere do we find the mouth of God promising paradise to a human being after Adam was cast out, except first to this thief. Why did he not speak of paradise first to any of the patriarchs, to any of the prophets, to any of the apostles? To the ancients he promised, "I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey"; to the apostles he says, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"; paradise nowhere. He keeps paradise in reserve in the meantime, to be promised first to the thief. For when Paul says, "I was caught up into paradise," that happened after the thief. Why, then, was the man who uttered just a single sentence the first to enter? What had he done? Had he sung psalms many times? Had he struggled many times? Had he spoken of God many times? "Only once," he says. My God, who awards the prize of salvation, is just: since he cast the first man, Adam, out of paradise not for many sins but for a single disobedience, so the scale of justice promised that the thief would be the first to enter paradise, the one who had not confessed many things but had offered a single confession of faith. I have named Adam's sin: that he touched the tree against the commandment. What is the thief's justification? That he touched the cross with faith, and so he entered paradise. What happens next? The Savior had promised salvation, but there was no time, nor was the thief given the chance to believe and be illumined. For the Savior had declared, "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven." The thief could find no opportunity or freedom; he had no time to be baptized, for he was hanging on the cross. So the Savior finds a way where there was none. Since the man who had grown old in sin had believed in the Savior and needed to be cleansed, Christ arranges that after his passion the soldier should pierce the Lord's side with the lance, and blood and water gush out. "For from his side," says the evangelist, "came out blood and water," as reality for the one who had fallen [?], and as a figure of the mysteries. And the blood and water did not simply flow out, but came out in a rushing stream, so as to sprinkle the thief's body. For what is shot out with force sprinkles, whereas what flows gently simply runs as it comes. But the blood and water came out of his side with force, so that by sprinkling the thief it might baptize him, as the apostle also says: "We have come to Mount Zion, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than the blood of Abel." Why does the blood of Christ speak better than that of Abel? Because the blood of Abel is on the murderer's head, while the blood of Christ cleanses even murderers who repent. So learn zeal for the truth, and love boldness of speech on behalf of Christ. Follow a true teacher who contends for the truth, so that, hearing the apostle Paul say, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ," you too may be found worthy of the crowns of righteousness and of the eternal blessings that Christ our God has prepared for those who love him. May we all attain them, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
